source: Original wording written for this app. The structure follows the four systems (Leads, Sales, Delivery, Profit) and twelve playbook titles of the ACQ playbook binder that shipped with the $100M Money Models launch; the ideas come from the published $100M books and Acquisition.com's public material. No text of any book or playbook is reproduced here.
confidenceNote: The exercises are a workbook reading of public frameworks, not the playbooks themselves. Rules of thumb in the copy (three to one, five minutes, nine touches, thirty days) are stated as rules of thumb.
note: Read by binders/app.js and binders/engines/reads.js. Twelve playbooks (planets) in four systems, six bands each: the same band means the same depth on every planet. A level is done when every exercise holds an answer and every checklist item is ticked. Exercise keys are unique across the file; a key marked shared is owned here and read elsewhere through { ref }. Money is typed in dollars and stored in integer cents.

bands.name: Read
bands.meaning: The one idea, and where you stand on it today

bands.name: Facts
bands.meaning: The few numbers this playbook runs on

bands.name: Exercises
bands.meaning: The pen and paper work the playbook asks for

bands.name: Build
bands.meaning: Assemble the thing you will use, and tick it off

bands.name: Run
bands.meaning: Use it for a stretch and log what happened

bands.name: Sharpen
bands.meaning: The moves only visible once the numbers are real

systems.label: Leads
systems.question: How do strangers find out you exist?

systems.label: Sales
systems.question: How does a stranger become a customer?

systems.label: Delivery
systems.question: How does a customer stay and bring more?

systems.label: Profit
systems.question: How does each customer pay for the next?

playbooks.label: Marketing Machine
playbooks.oneLine: Four ways to let people know you exist, and how much of each you need.
playbooks.idea: Advertising is letting people know about the thing you sell. There are only four ways to do it: reach out to people who already know you, post content for people who do not know you yet, reach out cold to strangers, and pay to put your message in front of them. Anyone else who gets you leads is doing one of those four on your behalf. The machine is the amount of each you do every day, on purpose, counted.

levels.title: The four ways, and what you do now
levels.why: Most lead problems are volume problems wearing a strategy costume. Before choosing anything, write down what actually happened last week.

exercises.label: How steady is your lead flow, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: What you did last week to get leads, literally
exercises.help: How many messages, how many posts, how many cold contacts, how many dollars. Count, do not describe.

exercises.label: The channel that brings most of your leads today
options: Warm outreach: people who know me
Content: posting for people who do not know me yet

checklist: I can name the four ways to get leads without looking
I wrote what I actually did last week, not what I meant to do
levels.checkpoint: The planet shows where you start and the four ways are named.

levels.title: The weekly counts
levels.why: A machine has dials. These are the dials: how much of each way you do in a normal week, and how many people raise a hand because of it.

exercises.label: Warm reach-outs per week
exercises.help: Messages to people who already know you: contacts, followers, past customers.

exercises.label: Pieces of content per week
exercises.help: Posts, emails, videos: anything for people who do not know you yet.

exercises.label: Cold contacts per week
exercises.help: Strangers you reached out to first: calls, DMs, emails, doors.

exercises.label: Ad spend per week
exercises.help: Dollars paid for attention. Zero is a number; leave it blank if you do not know.

exercises.label: Engaged leads per month
exercises.help: People who replied, booked, or opted in. A view is not a lead.

exercises.label: New customers you want per month
exercises.help: The target the machine has to produce.

checklist: Every count comes from a log, a sent folder or a receipt, not from memory
levels.checkpoint: The machine mix draws, and the leads-needed figure computes once Closing and Lead Nurture have their rates.

levels.title: The warm list, the topics, the cold sources
levels.why: Warm outreach is the cheapest lead you will ever get, and almost nobody does it fully. Content starts with questions you already get asked. Cold outreach starts with a list that already exists somewhere.

exercises.label: Your warm list, one name a line
exercises.help: Everyone who has your number, follows you, or has emailed you. Aim for 100. Stop when you run out, not when you get bored.

exercises.label: Ten things a customer asked you this month, one a line
exercises.help: Each is a piece of content. Their question is the hook.

exercises.label: Three places a list of your strangers already exists
exercises.help: A directory, a group, a conference list, a public register.

exercises.label: The one channel you will max out first
exercises.help: One. The rule is: max one channel before adding the next.

checklist: The warm list is every name I have, not a sample
The ten topics are real questions, in the words they were asked
levels.checkpoint: Three lists exist and one channel is chosen.

levels.title: The daily minimum
levels.why: A number you hit every day beats a plan you admire. Write the minimum as counts per day, then put someone in charge of it, even if that someone is you on Friday.

exercises.label: Your daily advertising minimum
exercises.help: Per day: how many warm messages, how many pieces of content, how many cold contacts, how many ad dollars. Small and daily beats big and monthly.

exercises.label: Where the daily count is logged
exercises.help: A sheet, a note, a wall. It has to exist before day one.

checklist: A place to log every day's count exists
The warm list has 100 names or every name I have
The first channel has a daily number attached
Someone is accountable for the number by Friday, even if it is me
The minimum is small enough to hit on a bad day
levels.checkpoint: The plan is written and the log is ready.

levels.title: Run it for two weeks
levels.why: Now the machine gets numbers of its own. Count reach and count leads. The ratio between them is the first honest reading of your message.

exercises.label: Days you ran the daily minimum
Contacts made in the run
exercises.help: Every warm message, post, cold contact and thousand ad views, all counted as one each.

exercises.label: Engaged leads from the run
exercises.help: Replied, booked or opted in.

exercises.label: Days the minimum was actually hit

checklist: The daily minimum was hit at least four days in five
levels.checkpoint: Your lead rate shows beside the rate you had before.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.why: When the machine works a little, the temptation is to add a channel. The rule is: more of the same first, then better, then new. Lead getters (customers who refer, employees, agencies, affiliates) are the four ways done by other people.

exercises.label: The next move
options: More: double the volume on the same channel
Better: fix the message, same volume
New: add the next channel, keep this one running
exercises.help: Take More unless volume is truly maxed. Take New last.

exercises.label: One person for each lead getter that applies
exercises.help: A past customer who would refer, an employee who could do outreach, an agency, an affiliate. Name a real person or write none.

checklist: I doubled the volume before I changed the channel
A referral ask is written into the delivery (see Retention)
The weekly counts are on the scorecard (see Implementation SOPs)
levels.checkpoint: The next move is decided and a lead getter is named.

playbooks.label: Hooks
playbooks.oneLine: The first line earns the second. Nothing you make gets read without one.
playbooks.idea: A hook is the part of a message people see before they decide whether to keep going: the headline, the first sentence, the first second of a video, the subject line. Most attention is lost right there. The work is not to write one good hook and hope. It is to write many, score them, run the best few, and keep the winners in a bank you draw on for years.

levels.title: Read your last three first lines as a stranger
levels.why: You cannot fix what you have not looked at. Pull up the last three things you sent or posted and read only the first line of each.

exercises.label: How often does what you post or send get a reply or a click, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: Your last three hooks, pasted in
exercises.help: The headline, the first line, the subject line. As they were, not as you would fix them.

checklist: I read my last three first lines as a stranger would
I can say who each one was for
levels.checkpoint: Your starting point on the planet is set.

levels.title: Last week's attention
levels.why: Two counts turn a feeling into a rate: how many people saw the first line, and how many did anything after it.

exercises.label: Views or opens last week, total
exercises.help: Across every post, email and ad.

exercises.label: Replies, clicks or saves last week, total
Hooks you drafted last week
exercises.help: Drafts, not posts. Zero is a number.

checklist: The counts come from the platform, not a guess
levels.checkpoint: Your hook rate shows.

levels.title: Twenty hooks for one idea
levels.why: Volume is the method. Twenty hooks for one idea, using different frames, gets you two good ones. One hook gets you one hope.

exercises.label: Who it is for, in the words they use for themselves
The one fact or result that backs the idea
exercises.help: A number, a name, a before and after. If there is none, see Proof Checklist.

exercises.label: Twenty hooks for the idea, one a line
exercises.help: Frames to rotate: a question, a number, a claim with a condition, a common mistake, a before and after, a call-out of who it is for, a short story opener.

checklist: All twenty are for the same idea
At least five different frames were used
None promises more than the proof can back
levels.checkpoint: A hook bank exists.

levels.title: Pick three and place them
levels.why: Score each hook on four things: it is specific, it is for someone, it makes you curious, and it is true. Take the top three, and make sure they are three different frames, not one hook three ways.

exercises.label: Your top three, one a line, highest score first
Where the three will run

checklist: Each of the three names who it is for or what it is about in the first five words
None of the three promises something the proof cannot back
The three are different frames, not one hook three ways
Each one is scheduled to run at least three times
levels.checkpoint: Three hooks are placed and scheduled.

levels.title: Run the three
levels.why: Run each hook enough times to compare. Count the same thing for each: replies, clicks or saves. Then write the count beside each hook.

exercises.label: Times the three ran in total
exercises.help: Posts sent, emails sent, or ad views in hundreds.

exercises.label: Replies, clicks or saves the three got, total
Each hook with its count, hook | count
exercises.help: One a line. The bar beside it draws from the number after the bar.

checklist: Each hook ran at least three times before I judged it
levels.checkpoint: Before and after hook rates sit side by side, and the three are ranked.

levels.title: Keep the winners, mark the losers
levels.why: A hook that beat the average goes in the bank and gets reused. A hook that lost goes in the bank too, marked, so you never rewrite it by accident.

exercises.label: Winners to keep in the bank, one a line
exercises.help: Used more than once and beat the average.

exercises.label: What to change next

checklist: Winning hooks are in a bank I can open in ten seconds
Losing hooks are in the bank too, marked as losers
Next week's twenty are on the calendar
levels.checkpoint: The bank has winners and the next twenty are scheduled.

playbooks.label: Lead Nurture
playbooks.oneLine: A lead is a person who raised a hand. The next hour and the next thirty days decide whether it counts.
playbooks.idea: Most leads are lost between the hand-raise and the conversation. Speed is the first lever: a reply inside minutes is worth many replies tomorrow. Persistence is the second: most people need to hear from you more times than feels polite, and they are not annoyed, they are busy. A lead magnet, a small free thing that solves one narrow problem and shows the next one, gives every follow-up a reason to exist.

levels.title: What happens when a hand goes up
levels.why: Time it. Count it. Most people are shocked by both numbers the first time they look.

exercises.label: How fast and how many times a new lead hears from you, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: What happens today when someone raises a hand
exercises.help: Who replies, in how long, how many times, with what. Step by step.

checklist: I timed my last reply to a new lead
I counted how many touches a lead gets before I stop
levels.checkpoint: Your starting point on the planet is set.

levels.title: Speed, touches, and the booking rate
levels.why: Three numbers describe the whole system: how fast, how many times, and what share of leads end up in a conversation.

exercises.label: Minutes from hand-raise to first reply, typical
exercises.help: In working hours. Look at the last five leads and take the middle one.

exercises.label: Touches a lead gets before you stop
exercises.help: Messages, calls, emails: every attempt counts as one.

exercises.label: Of engaged leads, the share who book a conversation
exercises.help: Booked, not shown. Showing is measured in Closing Handbook.

checklist: The reply time is measured from five real leads, not one
levels.checkpoint: Reply speed and the booking rate show.

levels.title: The magnet, the sequence, the short check-in
levels.why: A lead magnet is a free thing that solves a narrow problem completely and reveals the next problem, which your paid thing solves. The sequence is the nine or so touches after it. The short check-in is the one-line question you send to every lead that has gone quiet.

exercises.label: Your lead magnet kind
options: Reveal a problem they did not know they had: an audit, a score, a checklist
A sample or trial of the real thing
One step of a multi-step result: the first week, the first tool

exercises.label: Name it as the result it gives
exercises.help: Not what it is, what they get.

exercises.label: The follow-up sequence, one touch a line: day, channel, what it says
exercises.help: Aim for nine touches over thirty days, on at least two channels. Every touch has one ask.

exercises.label: Your short check-in for a quiet lead
exercises.help: One question, under fifteen words, easy to answer with one word.

checklist: The magnet solves its problem completely, not a teaser
The sequence uses at least two channels
Every touch has exactly one ask
levels.checkpoint: The magnet, the sequence and the check-in are written.

levels.title: Put a person on the five minutes
levels.why: Speed is a staffing decision. Someone gets told about every new lead, and answers inside five minutes in working hours. The sequence is scheduled, not remembered.

exercises.label: Who replies to a new lead within five minutes, and how they find out
exercises.help: A name and a notification. If it is you, say what buzzes.

exercises.label: Where the sequence is scheduled
exercises.help: A tool, a calendar, a checklist on the wall.

checklist: The lead magnet exists and can be sent as one link
Every new lead gets a reply within five minutes in working hours
The nine touches are scheduled, not remembered
Every quiet lead gets the short check-in after thirty days
Every touch has one ask
levels.checkpoint: The system runs without anyone remembering it.

levels.title: Thirty days of leads
levels.why: Now measure the same three numbers on leads that went through the new sequence. Log how many replied at each touch: that curve tells you where the sequence earns its keep.

exercises.label: Leads that entered the sequence in the run
Of those, how many booked a conversation
Median minutes to first reply in the run
Replies by touch
exercises.help: One row a touch: how many were sent that touch, how many replied to it.

checklist: The run covered at least thirty days so the late touches had time to land
levels.checkpoint: Before and after booking rates, reply speed, and the touch curve all show.

levels.title: Faster, more, better, or reactivate
levels.why: With a curve in hand the next move is obvious. If late touches still get replies, add more. If nobody replies after touch two, fix the magnet. And the old list is the cheapest campaign you will ever run.

exercises.label: The next move
options: Faster: cut the reply time in half
Reactivate: send the short check-in to the whole old list

exercises.label: Leads on the old list who never bought
exercises.help: They get the short check-in this month.

checklist: The old list got the short check-in this month
The magnet's next-problem points at the paid thing
Reply time is on the weekly scorecard
levels.checkpoint: The next move is decided and the old list is in play.

playbooks.label: Closing Handbook
playbooks.oneLine: A sale is a conversation with a shape. Learn the shape and the pressure goes out of it.
playbooks.idea: The conversation runs in six moves, and the letters spell CLOSER: clarify why they came, label the problem back to them in their words, overview what they have tried and why it did not hold, sell the outcome and not the method, explain away the concerns that remain, and reinforce the decision the moment they say yes. Concerns come in three kinds: about circumstances (time, money), about other people (a partner, a boss), and about themselves (fit, doubt). Each kind has an answer you write once and say many times.

levels.title: Your last conversation, in six lines
levels.why: Write up your last sales conversation from open to close. Where did it drift? Where did you talk most? Where did you lose them, if you did?

exercises.label: How confident are you in a sales conversation, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: Your last sales conversation, open to close, in six lines
exercises.help: One line per move if you can. If you cannot find six moves, that is the finding.

checklist: I recorded or wrote up my last call
I know where in the call I lose people
levels.checkpoint: Your starting point on the planet is set.

levels.title: The funnel of one month
levels.why: Booked, shown, bought, paid. Four counts make three rates, and each rate has its own playbook.

exercises.label: Conversations booked last month
Of those, how many showed up
Of those, how many bought
Cash collected at the close last month, total
exercises.help: What actually arrived, not what was promised.

checklist: The four counts come from a calendar and a bank statement, not memory
levels.checkpoint: Show rate, close rate and cash per sale show, and the Marketing Machine can compute leads needed.

levels.title: Write your six moves
levels.why: One paragraph per letter, in your own words, as you would say it to a friend across a table.

exercises.label: Clarify: the two questions you open with
exercises.help: Why now? What made you reach out? Their answer is the rest of the call.

exercises.label: Label: the sentence that names their problem back to them
exercises.help: In their words. Then ask: is that right?

exercises.label: Overview: the question that draws out what they tried and why it did not hold
exercises.help: The point is that they hear themselves say it.

exercises.label: Sell the vacation: the outcome, in three sentences, with no method in it
exercises.help: The beach, not the plane.

exercises.label: Explain away: your answer to each of the three kinds of concern
exercises.help: Circumstances (time, money). Other people (a partner, a boss). Themselves (fit, doubt). One answer each.

exercises.label: Reinforce: what happens in the first 24 hours after yes
exercises.help: A message, a call, a small gift. The decision needs a second yes from their future self.

checklist: Each move is written as I would say it, not as a script sounds
The label uses their words, not mine
levels.checkpoint: The six moves exist in your voice.

levels.title: One page, and the objection bank
levels.why: The script fits on one page or it will not be used. The objection bank grows after every call and never shrinks.

exercises.label: The objection bank: concern | your answer, one a line
exercises.help: Every concern you have ever heard, with the answer after the bar. Add to it after every call.

checklist: The script fits on one page
Every question in it is one I would ask a friend
The price is said once, plainly, with no apology
Silence after the price is written into the script
The three concern answers are memorised, not read
Reinforce happens the same day, every time
levels.checkpoint: The one-page script and the bank are ready.

levels.title: A month on the script
levels.why: Run the script on every conversation for a month. Count the same four things. Log which objections came up and how often you answered them well.

exercises.label: Conversations in the run
exercises.help: Shown, not booked.

exercises.label: Sales in the run
Cash collected at the close in the run, total
Objections heard
exercises.help: One row an objection.

checklist: Every conversation in the run used the script
One conversation a week was reviewed from a recording
levels.checkpoint: Before and after close rates, and the objection bars, show.

levels.title: Which rate, and who else can run it
levels.why: Each rate points at a different fix. And the script only counts once someone other than you can close with it.

exercises.label: The rate to work next
options: Show rate: fix the reminders before the call
Close rate: tighten the label and the overview
Cash rate: change the payment ask
Handoff: write the script so someone else can run it

exercises.label: Who runs the script next, other than you
exercises.help: A name, or none yet.

checklist: Calls are recorded and one a week is reviewed
The objection bank grew after every call
Reinforce runs the same day, every time
Close rate is on the weekly scorecard
levels.checkpoint: The next rate to work is decided.

playbooks.label: Proof Checklist
playbooks.oneLine: People do not buy the promise. They buy the evidence that the promise held for someone like them.
playbooks.idea: Whether someone believes an outcome will happen for them is half of what a thing is worth to them. Proof moves that belief. It comes in kinds: results with a number, before and after pairs, named testimonials, third-party marks (reviews, press, credentials), and demonstrations. The checklist is a habit rather than a project: collect proof at every win, put a proof beside every claim, and match the kind of proof to the doubt it answers.

levels.title: Read your pitch as a doubter
levels.why: Open your sales page or your pitch and read it as someone who has been burned before. Mark every claim that has nothing beside it.

exercises.label: How much evidence backs your offer today, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: Every piece of proof you can put your hands on in five minutes
exercises.help: Screenshots, messages, reviews, numbers. List them.

checklist: I read my pitch as a doubter
I marked every claim with no proof beside it
levels.checkpoint: Your starting point on the planet is set.

levels.title: Count the proof by kind
levels.why: Five kinds, five counts. The shape of the count tells you what to collect next.

exercises.label: Results with a number
exercises.help: A client got X in Y. Counted individually.

exercises.label: Named testimonials, written or on video
Before and after pairs
exercises.help: Pictures, screenshots, two numbers.

exercises.label: Third-party marks
exercises.help: Reviews on a platform, press, credentials, awards.

exercises.label: Demonstrations
exercises.help: A free sample, a live walkthrough, a recorded one.

exercises.label: Customers you have served, total
exercises.help: Ever. The proof inventory is measured against this.

checklist: Each count is of things I could show today, not things I could get
levels.checkpoint: The proof inventory draws, by kind.

levels.title: Claims, doubts, and ten people to ask
levels.why: Every claim your offer makes needs a proof or a cut. Every doubt a buyer has needs a proof that answers it. And ten past customers are one message away from a testimonial.

exercises.label: Every claim your offer makes, one a line
The five doubts a buyer has before paying, in their words
exercises.help: Will it work for me? What if I fail? Is this person real?

exercises.label: Ten past customers to ask this week, one a line, with what to ask each for
exercises.help: Name | the specific result to ask about | the kind of proof (a number, a story, a screenshot).

checklist: The doubts are in the buyer's words, not mine
Each of the ten asks names a specific result
levels.checkpoint: Claims, doubts and the ask list exist.

levels.title: A proof beside every claim
levels.why: Map each claim to the proof beside it. A claim with nothing beside it is cut or held until the proof arrives.

exercises.label: Claim | the proof beside it | the kind, one a line
exercises.help: A claim with no proof gets the word cut after the bar.

exercises.label: Where the proof lives
exercises.help: One folder anyone on the team can reach.

checklist: Every claim has a proof beside it or is cut
The three biggest doubts each have a proof that answers them
Asking for proof happens at the moment of a win, inside the delivery
Proof is stored in one folder anyone on the team can reach
Every name and number in the proof is real and permitted
levels.checkpoint: Every live claim has evidence beside it.

levels.title: A week of asking
levels.why: Send the ten asks. Count what came back. Count where you placed it.

exercises.label: Testimonials asked for in the run
Testimonials received
Places proof was added
exercises.help: The page, the script, an ad, an email: each counts as one.

checklist: Every ask named a specific result
Every proof received was placed somewhere within a week
levels.checkpoint: The ask rate and the placements show.

levels.title: Numbers, faces, marks, or a guarantee
levels.why: The strongest proof for the biggest doubt is a promise you will make good on. A guarantee names the outcome and the term, and it is priced in.

exercises.label: The next kind to build
options: Numbers: turn stories into results with figures
Guarantee: back the biggest doubt with a promise

exercises.label: The guarantee, in one sentence
exercises.help: What outcome, by when, or what happens. Or none yet.

checklist: A proof ask is written into the delivery (see Retention)
The guarantee names the outcome and the term
Proof is refreshed every quarter, oldest out
levels.checkpoint: The next kind of proof is decided.

playbooks.label: GOATed Ads
playbooks.oneLine: A paid ad is a call-out, a reason, and an ask, bought by the thousand and judged by the cost of a customer.
playbooks.idea: Paid ads are the fourth of the four ways to get leads and the one that scales fastest once the math works. An ad has three parts: a call-out that says who it is for, value that gives them a reason to keep watching, and a call to action that says the one thing to do next. The math is a chain: cost per thousand views, the share who click, the share who become leads, the share who book, the share who buy. An ad is good when the lifetime gross profit of a customer is at least three times what it cost to get them.

levels.title: What you spend and what comes back
levels.why: Most people know their spend and not their cost per customer. Write the honest version, including "not yet".

exercises.label: How well do you know your cost per customer from ads, 1 to 5
exercises.help: One is not at all, five is fully. Your honest read today.

exercises.label: What you spend, where, and what you get, a sentence each
exercises.help: If you have never run an ad, write that, and write the top ad in your space in its three parts.

checklist: I have a number for cost per lead or I wrote not yet
I looked at the best ad in my space and wrote its three parts
levels.checkpoint: Your starting point on the planet is set.

levels.title: The chain, last month
levels.why: Six counts, from the platform and the calendar. Each link in the chain is a rate you can fix on its own.

exercises.label: Ad spend last month
Impressions last month
exercises.help: Times the ad was shown.

exercises.label: Clicks last month
Leads from ads last month
exercises.help: Opted in, replied or booked.

exercises.label: Conversations booked from ads last month
Customers from ads last month

checklist: The counts come from the platform and the calendar for the same month
levels.checkpoint: The chain draws, the costs compute, and the ratio shows once Lifetime Value has its facts.

levels.title: Ten call-outs, ten reasons, five asks
levels.why: Write the three parts separately and in volume. The best ad is a combination you have not tried yet.

exercises.label: Ten call-outs: who it is for, in their words, one a line
exercises.help: A job, a situation, a place, a thing they own, a thing they want.

exercises.label: Ten value lines: the reason to keep watching, one a line
exercises.help: A result, a mistake, a number, a story, a demonstration.

exercises.label: Five calls to action, one a line
exercises.help: One verb, one place, one reason to do it now.

checklist: Every call-out would make the right person stop
Every value line is a claim the proof can back (see Proof Checklist)
levels.checkpoint: The parts exist in volume.

levels.title: The ad, in three versions
levels.why: Assemble one ad from the parts, then two more with different hooks and the same offer. The landing place has to say the same thing as the ad.

exercises.label: The ad, written out: call-out, value, call to action

playbooks.label: Retention
playbooks.oneLine: Keeping a customer is the cheapest sale you will ever make. The first days decide it.
playbooks.idea: Every month a share of customers leave. That share sets how long an average customer stays: one divided by the monthly churn. Churn is highest early, so the first days matter most: a fast first win, a clear next step, and a person who checks in. Most churn has a reason you can name, and the reasons cluster. Count them, fix the biggest, and ask the ones who stay to bring a friend.

playbooks.label: Lifetime Value
playbooks.oneLine: What a customer is worth over their whole stay, in gross profit. Every other number answers to this one.
playbooks.idea: Lifetime gross profit is what a customer pays you over their stay, minus what it costs to deliver to them. It is the price, times the gross margin, times how many times they buy. There are only four ways to raise it: more customers, more per purchase, more purchases, and a longer stay. Know the number, then compare it to what a customer costs to get. Three to one is the rule of thumb below which a business feels like a treadmill.

playbooks.label: Branding
playbooks.oneLine: A brand is what people already like, tied to your name, on purpose, over and over.
playbooks.idea: A brand is an association: you, paired with things a group of people already wants, enough times that the pairing sticks. It is built by choosing who you are for, what you stand beside, and what you will never do, and then being boringly consistent about all three. The test is simple: can a customer describe you in one sentence, and does it match the sentence you wrote.

playbooks.label: Price Raise
playbooks.oneLine: Most businesses are underpriced. The math says how many customers you can lose on a raise and still come out ahead.
playbooks.idea: Price is the number the value earns. When you raise it some customers leave, and the question is how many you can lose before the raise stops paying. With a gross margin, the breakeven loss is the raise divided by the margin plus the raise: at a 70 percent margin, a 20 percent raise can lose about a fifth of customers and make the same profit. Raise price after you have raised value, tell existing customers before, and give them a reason the new price is fair.

playbooks.label: Promo Cash
playbooks.oneLine: Make more from a customer in the first thirty days than it costs to get and serve them. Then growth pays for itself.
playbooks.idea: A money model is the order of offers a customer meets. It starts with an attraction offer that gets a stranger to say yes: win your money back, a free thing with a string attached, a discount for a commitment, a giveaway, or a decoy beside the real thing. Then the offers that follow: an upsell at the moment of yes, a downsell for the no, and continuity so the money keeps arriving. The target is that the gross profit collected in the first thirty days is more than it cost to acquire and deliver. Then every customer funds the next one.

playbooks.label: Implementation SOPs
playbooks.oneLine: A playbook only counts when someone other than you can run it. Write it down, give it a number, look at the number weekly.
playbooks.idea: The other eleven playbooks each end with a thing to run and a number to watch.
